title: What may be sung
hookLine: only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal are sung in kirtan

cards: A harmonium wheezes into its first chord. A tabla player taps the skin twice to check the pitch.

Three singers sit cross-legged on a low platform to the side of the Granth, and the hall goes quiet the way a hall does when music is about to start. One question was answered long before anyone sat down. Not which tune.
Not which instrument. Which words. The code is strict about it, and the strictness tells you something about what a sung line can do to a person.

teach.h: KIRTAN: THE SUNG PRAISE OF GOD.
teach.b: The singing is called kirtan, the sung praise of God.

teach.h: ONLY GURBANI, AND TWO WHO EXPLAIN IT.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the code says that in the sangat, kirtan is to be only of Gurbani, the Gurus' own words, or of the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, which explain Gurbani. That's the whole list.
A gifted singer doesn't perform a hymn they wrote last week, however moving it is. A well-known poem doesn't get in because it's beautiful. Why draw the line so tight?
Go back to the sangat, and Guru Nanak's test: the true company is known by what is said there.
A melody is glue for words. A tune can carry a line long after the page is closed. Whatever is sung in the hall is what the sangat will hum in the kitchen, on the drive home, at the hospital bed.

So the code guards the words, because the words are what the music will plant. Now the two names on the list. Bhai Gurdas was a Sikh scholar and poet close to the Gurus; tradition calls his writing a key to Gurbani.

Bhai Nand Lal was a poet in the Tenth Guru's court, the one met with the poets of Anandpur. Neither is a Guru. Their works are allowed as explanation, so even the exceptions point back to the Guru's word.
This is a rule for kirtan in the sangat, not a rule that Sikhs never write or sing anything else.
Poetry, folk songs and new music all have their places in Sikh life. But in the hall, in front of the Granth, the voice belongs to the Guru.

how: In the gurdwara, ragis sing kirtan from Gurbani, sometimes with the works of Bhai Gurdas or Bhai Nand Lal, usually with harmonium and tabla; the words are often shown on a screen for the sangat to follow.

games.q: what does “what may be sung” mean?
o: the hymns of the Tenth Guru, and none of the others
only Gurbani and the works that explain it, in kirtan
any song with a good tune, in any language

games.q: what may be sung: tap the pairs.
p: a poet whose works explain Gurbani
a poet in the Tenth Guru's court

s: in the sangat, a singer may perform a new hymn of their own as kirtan
the code allows only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal.
the code allows Bhai Gurdas's and Bhai Nand Lal's works in kirtan
allowed because they explain Gurbani; even the exceptions point back to the Guru's word.
the rule means Sikhs may never sing any other song anywhere
it's a rule for kirtan in the sangat. poetry and other music have their places in Sikh life.

games.q: a gifted poet writes a moving new hymn and asks to sing it as kirtan in the sangat. what does the code say?
o: yes, if the sangat finds it beautiful.
no: kirtan is Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal.
games.why: the code keeps kirtan to Gurbani and the two poets who explain it. the voice in the hall belongs to the Guru.

practice: Bring up a song that's been stuck in your head lately and, without judging it, say its words slowly without the tune, asking whether you'd choose to repeat them all day.
If you know a line of Gurbani, or a line from any text you love, let it play instead and notice how it sits.

wordCard.voice: What may be sung. In the sangat, kirtan is only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, which explain it. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the sung praise of God; in the sangat, Gurbani set to music.

carryVoice: Your line: only the word. Next comes one hymn that the reader doesn't choose. Until tomorrow.
